entries.english: A small group of people lifts the heavy wooden mortar. (Many hands make light work.)
One finger cannot kill (crush) a louse. (No man is an island / Two heads are better than one.)
One log alone does not keep the fire burning through the night. (United we stand, divided we fall.)
A single peg cannot stretch out an animal hide. (It takes a village.)
Two honey badgers are not defeated by a beehive. (Union is strength.)
The wisdom of one person alone does not cultivate a field. (In the multitude of counsellors there is safety.)
One does not ask for news from a hungry person (or: Hunger is not interrogated). (A hungry belly has no ears.)
Goodness (generosity and good character) begins at home. (Charity begins at home.)
Whoever walks with a corrupt/tainted person becomes tainted like them. (Birds of a feather flock together / Bad company corrupts good character.)
Like the yam vine and the mũkũngũgũ support tree. (Inseparable companions / Thick as thieves.)
No day dawns exactly like another. (Every day brings its own dawn.)

entries.english: The 10 Chronological Ages Since Creation (Rĩĩka) & Generational Transfer (Ai-twi-ka / Itwika, Routledge 1910, p. 9)
entries.translation: 1. Man-jí-ri (God spoke to first man Mam'-ba, who told his son N'jí-ri to dig channels and drain the earth) → 2. Man-dó-ti (age of evildoers) → 3. Chi-éra (people increased greatly) → 4. Masaí (smearing with red earth became fashionable) → 5. Ma-thá-thi (Akikúyu came from the Akam'ba) → 6. N'dé-mi ('to cut' — Akikúyu cut forest trees) → 7. entries.translation: Jogowini Dialect & 6 Plural Classes (pp. vi–vii): recorded by Hildegarde Hinde at Fort Hall (Sept. 1902); (1) mu- → a- (muka → aka, Mukikuyu → Akikuyu), (2) mu- → mi- (muti → miti), (3) i- → ma- (ihiga → mahiga), (4) ki- → i- (kiratu → iratu), (5) n- invariable (nyumba), (6) ka-/ki- → twa-/shi- (kana → twana/siana, kiara → shiara) • Complete Ku-tinda ('to conquer') Paradigm (pp. xii–xviii): Present n-a-tinda; Present Imperfect ni-ki-tinda; Present Perfect ni-tind-eti/-iti; Past Perfect ni-tind-eri, wa/u-tind-eri, a-tind-eri, tu-tind-eri, mu-tind-eri, me/ma-tind-eri; Future ni/nin-ka/ga-tinda (conversational nin-ku-shoka 'I will return'); Imperative tinda! (pl. tindani! / tindai!); Subjunctive ni-tinde; Negative Present n-di-tinda; Negative Past Perfect n-di-na-tinda; Negative Future n-di-ka/ga-tinda; Negative Imperative di/ndi-tinda!; Negative Subjunctive n-di-tinde • Six Age-Grade Dances & 2 War-Songs (pp. 17, 65): muthun guuchi (elders' dance), ngushu (children's dance), kishukia (warriors' dance), nduumo (young women's dance), kitiiro (old women's dance), reegu (uncircumcised boys' dance); War-songs (p. 65): nduugu (sung when going to war) vs. karre (sung when returning from war) • Traditional Ear Ornaments & Salutation (pp. 15, 21, 75): thūmbi (colobus monkey head-dress), ndĕbe (round ear-lobe ornaments), nyorri (curved or double ear-sticks), ichuhi (women's earrings), ndugirri (top edge of ear), mōnni (ear-lobe), ūttu (hole in ear-lobe); Salutation (p. 75): mwohoro! — Reply: mwohoro mwēga! / mwēga munnu!
entries.pronunciation: mu-ki-ku-yu a-ki-ku-yu / ni-tind-e-ri / ki-shu-kia / nduu-mo / ki-tii-ro / mwo-ho-ro mwe-ga
entries.context: Hildegarde Hinde (1904) 'Vocabularies of the Kamba and Kikuyu Languages of East Africa', pp. v–xviii, 2–75

entries.english: Aboriginal Forest Predecessors of the Akikúyu: The A'si (A-ki-e-ki / N'doróbo) & Pit-Dwelling A-gum'-ba (Routledge 1910, pp. 3–6, 39)
entries.translation: A'si / A-ki-e-ki (N'doróbo forest hunters from whom the Akikúyu purchased forest clearings for ~30 goats) • A-gum'-ba (also called A-mai-tho ma chi-a-na / Maitho ma chi-a-na = 'enemies of the children' or 'children’s eyes', dwarfish 4 ft 6 in pit-hut dwellers who dug circular pits on ridges, roofed them with poles and earth, used obsidian implements and wild banana seeds Pl. CVI, and vanished westward)
entries.pronunciation: a-si / a-ki-e-ki / a-gum-ba / a-mai-tho ma chi-a-na
entries.context: W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910) 'With a Prehistoric People', Ch. I, pp. 3–6, 39 & Plate CVI

entries.english: 10 Male & 7 Female Life-Stage Terms in W. S. & K. Routledge (1910, pp. 25, 139, 141, 171, 367–380)
entries.translation: 10 Male Life Stages (p. 25): 1. Ka'-he (small boy) → 2. Ki'-he (pl. i'-hee, big uninitiated boy) → 3. Mu'-mo (newly circumcised youth) → 4. M'wa-na'-ke (adult warrior) → 5. Wa-ka-ny-u-ku (newly married man) → 6. Mun'-du mu-ge'-ma (married man with a child) → 7. Ka-ra-bai' (married man whose children are growing up) → 8. M'zur'-i (elderly man / father of circumcised child) → 9. M'zur'-i a ki-a-na (elderly man needing a walking stick) → 10. M'zur'-i a bou'i (tottering white-headed old man) • 7 Female Life Stages (p. 141): 1. Ka-re'-go (small girl) → 2. Ki-ré-gu / Ki-ri'-gu (big uninitiated girl) → 3. Moi-re'-tu (pl. ai-, initiated maiden) → 4. Mu-hi'-ki (betrothed/married woman not yet a mother) → 5. Wa-bai / M'wa-na-mú-ke (mother of young children) → 6. Mu-ti-mi'-a / Mu-te-mi-a (mother of an initiated child, who shaves her head completely and wears ki-chan'-ga copper earrings) → 7. I-he'-ti (toothless old woman, revered as 'filled with intelligence' and accorded burial, pp. 139, 171)
entries.pronunciation: ka-he, ki-he, mu-mo, m-wa-na-ke, m-zur-i, ka-re-go, ki-re-gu, moi-re-tu, mu-hi-ki, mu-ti-mi-a, i-he-ti
entries.context: W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910) 'With a Prehistoric People', pp. 25, 139, 141, 171, 367–380

entries.english: Official Ranks (Mo-ran'-ja, Ki-á-ma, N'já-ma), Ceremonial Ox-Division & Wergild Scale (Routledge 1910, pp. 44, 195–220)
entries.translation: Three Official Ranks (pp. 196–205): 1. Mo-ran'-ja (called N'dun'-du in Karúri’s district, Ke-thi-ga near Nairobi: 1st rank entered by father of a 2nd child upon paying 2–3 sheep) → 2. Ki-á-ma (council of elders/judges, entered by father of a circumcised child paying 1 goat to N'jáma and 2 goats to Kiáma; carries staff of Mu-ti'-gi, Mun'-deren'-du, or Mú-ta-zi, wears ki-chan'-go earring, and carries Ma-tu-ra N'gu-ru leaves) → 3. N'já-ma (co-opted executive & police council of warriors; chief = Mu-tha-má-ki, spokesman = Mo-chí-ri) • Ceremonial Ox Division (p. 202): N'jáma = breast; Kiáma = belly & saddle; Moran'ja = back; Young men = head, neck & ribs; Women = inside • Wergild, Fines & Bridewealth (pp. 44, 215): Killing a man = 100–120 goats + 1 cow (or 9 milk goats / 9 sheep); killing a woman = 30–40 goats (+ 6 sheep); loss of arm or leg = 40–60 goats; whole finger = 30 goats; each finger joint = 10 goats; marriage marli = 30 goats + 5–6 sheep (1 cow = 13 goats; 1 goat = 120 n'da-ra skewered meat pieces, p. 59)
entries.pronunciation: mo-ran-ja, n-dun-du, ki-a-ma, n-ja-ma, mu-tha-ma-ki, mo-chi-ri, n-da-ra
entries.context: W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910) 'With a Prehistoric People', pp. 44, 59, 195–220

entries.english: 11 Traditional Dances, 6 Transcribed Songs (Dr. C. S. Myers), Picture-Rattle (Ki-shan'-di) & 5 Guso Riddles (Routledge 1910, pp. 109–116, 178–192)
entries.translation: 11 Dances by Age & Sex (p. 179): Boys = Ke-boí-i-a, N'goi-í-sa, Mam-bú-ra (great pre-initiation gathering displaying m'wen-gu wooden shield-arch and ma-rú-ngai oval plank shields, pp. 156–164); Men = N'dor-ó-si (forbidden in fort), Ki-bá-ta / N'di'-ri, and Maize-harvest dance with clay figurine; Men & Women = Mui-goí-o (performed at night holding burning brands), Ke-chú-ki-a, Ke-o-na-no, Ku-i-ne-né-ra; Women = Ge-ti-ro, N'dú-mo • Picture-Rattle Performance (pp. 109–112): ku-i'-nya ki-shan'-di (fee: 1 goatskin; Rattle I has 47 incised symbols & Rattle II has 37 symbols including Ndamathia snake, hyena-trap marīga, Orion’s belt mirī ya sulu, Pleiades kirīmera, honey-bird ngūhi, bamboo flute mūtūriru) • 6 Songs Notated by Dr. C. S. Myers (pp. 113–116): Ku-lan-gí-ri (hoeing song), Dú-mo (women’s marriage chorus), Mu-goí-i-o I & II, Ku-lu-mí-si-a (sick-cattle song), and War Song • 5 Verbatim Guso ('Do you hear?') Riddles (p. 192): (1) What hangs down? — Bananas; (2) Why do I hear a noise? — The birds are in the shamba; (3) What takes a winding course? — An N'doróbo on the road; (4) The young men go, the old men stay? — The ashes are poured out, the hearth-stones remain; (5) What goes from hill to hill? — The foot
entries.pronunciation: ke-boi-i-a, mam-bu-ra, ki-ba-ta, mui-goi-o, ge-ti-ro, n-du-mo, ki-shan-di, gu-so
entries.context: W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910) 'With a Prehistoric People', pp. 109–116, 156–164, 178–192

entries.english: Religion, Sacrifice to N'gaí (Mwi-nin-ya-ga), N'da-ma-thi-a River-Snake Worship, N'gor'o vs. N'góma, 29 Thá-hu Offences & Ki-tha-si (Routledge 1910, pp. 225–281)
entries.translation: Supreme Deity (pp. 225–236): N'gaí / Mwi-nin-ya-ga ('Possessor of Whiteness') dwelling on Ki-ri-nya-ga / Ki-re-í-ra (Mt. Kenya) and Ny-an-da-rou (Mt. Kinangop); sacrificed to beneath sacred Mu-gú-mu (Ficus) enclosed by 8 shrubs with responses 'N'ga-na!' (Amen) and 'Sa-i! Sa-i!' (Hear, hear!, p. 235) • Ai-twi-ka Snake Worship (pp. 237–238): river-creature N'da-ma-thi-a in the Mathioya River (in charge of Mu-tha-ka, held 1891 & 1903 near Chieftainess Wan'-go, lured out by two N'don-go-ru horns so hairs from its tail are plucked for generational blessing) • Soul vs. Ancestral Spirit (pp. 239–244): N'gor'o (living soul/heart/breath) vs. N'góma (ancestral spirit entering the ta-tu caterpillar, hyena, hun-gu kite, Mu-gú-mu tree, or hearth fire, and dwelling in the underworld Mi-i-ri-ni-ya Mi-kon-go-i) • 29 Causes of Thá-hu & Purification Formulas (pp. 256–263): 'Ta-hí-ka thá-hu!' ('Vomit the sin!'), 'Ta-hí-ka ki-ú-ru!' ('Expel what is bad!'), and 'Ni-da-ni-na thá-hu wa-ku' ('I have purged your sin', swept with 9-plant besoms) • Ki-tha-si Curse Stone (pp. 273–275): 14-holed ancient stone (7 holes on each side) held by De-gua wa Ki-ma-ni near Tú-su, invoked with 7 goats and 7 sticks
entries.pronunciation: n-gai, mwi-nin-ya-ga, n-da-ma-thi-a, n-gor-o, n-go-ma, mi-i-ri-ni-ya mi-kon-go-i, ta-hi-ka tha-hu, ki-tha-si
entries.context: W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910) 'With a Prehistoric People', Part III, Ch. XII–XIV, pp. 225–281

entries.english: Origin Myths & 13 Verbatim Folktales (Ro-gá-no, pl. N'gá-no) in W. S. & K. Routledge (1910, Part IV, pp. 283–328)
entries.translation: Origin Myths (pp. 283–284): Mt. Kenya created as God’s resting place when the earth was shallow water; Sun (husband) & Moon (wife) with Stars as Moon’s children, and Mu-ti-ru-m'we-ri (sacred day of rest after the dead moon) • 13 Folktales (pp. 285–328): 1. The Maiden Sacrificed for Rain (Wanjíru sinks into the ground and is rescued by her warrior lover); 2. The Lost Sister (Wagacharaíbu rescues M'wer'u; variant Wam'wéa & Wachéra); 3. The Four Young Warriors (killed by a falling rock after boasting and cursing the path); 4. Kacham'bi & the Kaniónikan'ga Bird (father killed by the giant bird, son Kacham'bi slays it and becomes chief); 5. Wanjíru & the Birds (du-tu-ra doves carry abused stepdaughter to a rich husband); 6. The Greedy Hyena, Sungúra (Hare) & Kihúru (Mongoose/Civet); 7. The Elephants & the Hyenas (hyena eats elephant’s marrow and carries the dead elephant on his head); 8. The Giant of the Great Water (Mukun'ga M'bura / Rainbow-Snake slain by surviving twin brother); 9. The Snake from the Great Water (marries Wadúa, slain by her brother Washúma with his sword); 10. M'wambía & the N'jengé (two-mouthed cannibal outwitted by the boy M'wambía); 11. The Girl who Cut the Hair of the N'jengé (Ilímu); 12. The Forty Girls (Washíshi rescues Moiréwanyína from the Ilímu’s bag); 13. The Man who Became a Hyena (Ilímu shape-shifter exposed by Wanjíru’s little brother)
entries.pronunciation: ro-ga-no, n-ga-no, wan-ji-ru, ka-cham-bi, mu-kun-ga m-bu-ra, n-jen-ge, i-li-mu
entries.context: W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910) 'With a Prehistoric People', Part IV: Folk-Lore, pp. 283–328

entries.english: Complete Material Culture, Dress, Craft & Ritual Glossary in W. S. & K. Routledge (1910, Glossaries pp. 367–380)
entries.translation: Dress & Ornaments: chiu-ma (small glass beads), gí-tá-li (zig-zag wire ornament), han-gí (string + wire beads), i-chú-hi (wedding finger ring), i-rú-tu (pl. ma-, earlobe plug of green leaves), ka-thí-ga (white stone shell bead), ke-nói-i (solid wooden ear cylinder), ki-chán-ga / ki-chán-go (wire ring with 3 blue beads worn by mothers of circumcised children & Kiáma elders), m'bu-gú-i (dancing belt of iron jingles), m'nior-o (chain earlobe ornament), mu-niún-gi (brass hoop earrings), mu-rín-ga (collars & bracelets of coiled wire), mu-thí-gi (long staff showing standard of life), n'dé-be (wood ring in perforated earlobe), n'gú-o (woman’s skin petticoat), nió-ri (3 small cane studs in upper ear), thum'-bi (ostrich/colobus warrior headdress) • Weapons, Ironwork & Crafts: ge-chú-hi (iron wedge for splitting logs), gi-ká-ma (slag/dross), í-ha (pig-skin quiver), i-rú-a (tweezers), ka-hiu' (razor), ke-gí-na (white sandy quartz iron ore), kí-gá-ro (barbed arrow-head), ki-rí-a (chisel), kir-í-ha (iron anvil; apprentice = mu-rú-gi), n'do-gó-ta (wooden spear-rest used until bridewealth is paid), n'dó-me (warrior’s arm-ring shield), n'gó-i (skin cradle for carrying baby on back), n'gó-zi (sheep-skin shoulder cape), niun'-gu (earthenware pot; broken potneck support = n'gá-ta), ro-híu (double-edged sword in crimson sheath chiu-ra), ru-kó-re (wooden spoon), ru-wén-gu (magical iron rod inherited from father), thé-gi (3-legged wooden stool carved in one piece), thu-rú-a (tuyere clay nozzle), u'-ta (bow) • Homestead, Food & Ritual: ché-hi (gruel of m'wé-le), ge-thú-no (meat feast structure in bush), gí-thá-ka (woodland estate), í-hé-ha (small sleeping hut for unmarried men), i-kúm-bi (granary basket), ki-gó-ro (hut shrine to N'gaí), ki-rá-ro (4-day seclusion in hut after birth), ku-hó-ya N'gaí (to pray/ask N'gaí), ku-rá-gu-ra (to divine), ku-ró-ga (to bewitch), ma-gón-gó-na (sacrifices to N'gaí), ma-hó-ri (lungs), m'bú-ri ya n'gó-ma (sacrifice to spirits), mo-ró-gi (poisoner/wizard), mu-chá-ri (wild date palm stripped for famine pith), mu-kí-ma (mashed banana & beans), mu-rá-tá-na (sausage tree Kigelia africana whose fruit ferments beer), mu-tú-ra (blood & mince-meat sausage), n'gá-ri (leopard, sacred animal across Kikúyu), n'gó-ni (special mark on tongue/teeth), n'jó-hi (sugar-cane beer), ny-úm-ba (woman’s hut), ru-én-i (cleared common grazing ground), thin-gí-ra (man’s hut), u-chú-ru (maize gruel)
